summary: Specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over FDDI networks and how link-local and autoconfigured addresses are formed there. It replaces RFC 2019. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: FDDI was a fast ring network that used glass cables. This says how to wrap IPv6 data to travel around such a ring.

questions: how is ipv6 carried over fddi
what is the default mtu for ipv6 over fddi
how is an ipv6 interface identifier made from a mac address
subtitle: How IPv6 packets are framed, addressed and mapped to link-layer addresses on FDDI networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a defined way to ride on each kind of link. FDDI needed a frame format, an MTU, a way to build interface identifiers and a way to map IPv6 addresses to FDDI addresses.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 packets go in LLC/SNAP frames with Ethertype 86DD, the default MTU is 4352 octets, the interface identifier is built from the 48-bit MAC address in EUI-64 form, and multicast uses addresses starting with 3333.
tldr.outcome: This memo replaces RFC 2019 and is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 2467 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2019, and it has been updated by RFC 8064.

sections.title: What the Memo Covers
sections.content:
This memo specifies three things for IPv6 on FDDI: the frame format for IPv6 packets, how to form link-local and statelessly autoconfigured addresses, and the contents of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages.

It replaces RFC 2019, 'Transmission of IPv6 Packets Over FDDI', which the text says will become historic. The term FDDI here includes CDDI.
sections.eli5: It is a short rulebook for sending IPv6 over one particular kind of network cable: what the envelope looks like, how a computer picks its name tag, and how to find a neighbour.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
FDDI allows a frame length of 4500 octets, including at least 22 octets of data link encapsulation when long-format addresses are used. After the 8 octets of LLC/SNAP header, that would in principle allow an IPv6 packet of up to 4470 octets. To leave room for variable MAC header sizes and future extensions of the frame status fields, the default MTU is 4352 octets.

The MTU may be lowered by a Router Advertisement carrying an MTU option, or by manual configuration. If an advertisement specifies an MTU larger than 4352 or larger than the manually configured value, the option may be logged to system management but must otherwise be ignored. Information received from DHCP counts as manually configured.
sections.eli5: The envelope has a size limit. The memo picks a safe size a little smaller than the largest possible, and it lets a router ask for smaller but never larger.

sections.title: Frame Format
sections.content:
FDDI offers synchronous and asynchronous transmission. Only asynchronous transmission with unrestricted tokens is required for interoperability, so IPv6 packets are sent in asynchronous frames using unrestricted tokens. Nodes should still be able to receive synchronous frames and asynchronous frames sent with restricted tokens.

Packets travel in LLC/SNAP frames using long-format (48 bit) addresses. The data field holds the IPv6 header and payload and is followed by the FDDI Frame Check Sequence, Ending Delimiter and Frame Status symbols. The header fields have fixed values: the Frame Code FC must be in the range 50 to 57 hexadecimal (the three low-order bits give the priority), DSAP and SSAP are both AA, CTL is 03 (Unnumbered Information), OUI is 000000 and the Ethertype is 86DD.
sections.eli5: Every packet goes into an envelope with a label saying 'this holds IPv6', so the receiving computer knows how to read what is inside.

sections.title: Interaction with Bridges
sections.content:
MAC bridges that join different media, for example Ethernet and FDDI, are very widespread. Some fragment IPv4 packets or support IPv4 Path MTU discovery, and many do not or do it incorrectly. Use of IPv6 in a bridged mixed-media environment must not depend on bridge support, unless the bridges are known to implement IPv6 Path MTU Discovery correctly.

When bridges lack that support, routers must advertise the smallest MTU of all the media in an MTU option. If no routers are present, that MTU must be configured by hand in each node attached to a medium whose default MTU is larger than the smallest one.
sections.eli5: If a mail chute between two buildings only fits small envelopes, everyone must use the small size, because the chute will not tell you when something is too big.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
The Interface Identifier for an FDDI interface is based on an EUI-64 identifier derived from the interface's built-in 48-bit IEEE 802 address. The first three octets of the MAC address (the OUI) become the company_id, the fourth and fifth octets of the EUI-64 are set to FFFE, and the last three MAC octets become the last three octets. The identifier is then obtained by complementing the Universal/Local bit, the next-to-lowest order bit of the first octet. The built-in address 34-56-78-9A-BC-DE gives 36-56-78-FF-FE-9A-BC-DE.

A MAC address set manually or by software should not be used to derive the identifier; if one must be used, its global uniqueness should be reflected in the U/L bit. A prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration on FDDI must be 64 bits long.

The link-local address is formed by appending the Interface Identifier to the prefix FE80::/64.
sections.eli5: A computer builds its own name tag from the serial number printed on its network card, with a few fixed digits added in the middle and one bit flipped. Nobody has to hand out names.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content:
Unicast mapping from IPv6 addresses to FDDI link-layer addresses follows Neighbor Discovery. The Source/Target Link-layer Address option has Type 1 for a source address or 2 for a target address, Length 1 (in units of 8 octets), and then the 48-bit FDDI address in canonical bit order. That address is the one the interface currently responds to, which may differ from the built-in address used to derive the Interface Identifier.

For multicast, an IPv6 packet with destination address DST is sent to the FDDI multicast address whose first two octets are 3333 hexadecimal and whose last four octets are the last four octets of DST (DST[13] through DST[16]).
sections.eli5: To find a neighbour's real card address you ask on the ring and they answer with it. For messages to a whole group, the group address is made by taking the last part of the IPv6 address and putting 3333 in front.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 2019
sections.content: The memo lists three functional changes from RFC 2019. 'FDDI adjacency detection' was removed because of recent work in IEEE 802.1p. The Address Token, which was a node's 48-bit MAC address, is replaced by the 64-bit Interface Identifier based on EUI-64. Prefixes used for stateless autoconfiguration must now be 64 bits long rather than 80, and the link-local prefix is likewise shortened to 64 bits.
sections.eli5: This is the list of things fixed since the first edition: one old feature dropped, and the name tags made longer and more standard.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Deriving Interface Identifiers from MAC addresses is intended to preserve global uniqueness where possible. The memo points out that there is no protection from duplication, whether by accident or by forgery.
sections.eli5: Name tags are built from card serial numbers, but nothing stops two cards from having the same one by mistake, or someone from faking it on purpose.
